cards.q: What is Git?
cards.a: Git is a version-control system: it records snapshots of a project so you can inspect, compare, share, and recover its history. It works locally first — you can commit without being online.

cards.q: Is Git the same thing as GitHub?
cards.a: No. Git is the version-control tool. GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, and similar services host Git repositories and add collaboration features such as issues, pull requests, permissions, and CI.

cards.q: What is a repository?
cards.a: A project folder whose history Git tracks. The hidden .git directory holds Git's objects, references, and configuration; the visible files are your working tree.

cards.q: What is a commit?
cards.a: A snapshot of the staged project, identified by its hash, plus metadata: its author, time, message, and parent commit or commits. A commit is local until you push it somewhere.

cards.q: Does Git continuously sync every edit?
cards.a: No. You choose what enters the next snapshot with git add, then record that snapshot with git commit. Publishing it with git push is a separate choice.

cards.q: What does Git track: files or changes?
cards.a: Git stores project snapshots. It can compare snapshots to describe additions, deletions, renames, and edits, but its core model is a history of complete states.

cards.q: What is the safest first command when you feel lost?
cards.a: git status. It reports the current branch and separates staged, unstaged, and untracked work. Read it before guessing at a fix.

cards.q: How do you check whether Git is installed?
cards.a: Run git --version. If it prints a version, the command is available.

cards.q: Which identity should you configure before committing?
cards.a: Set git config --global user.name "Your Name" and git config --global user.email "you@example.com". These become commit metadata; they are not login credentials.

cards.q: How do you make new repositories start on main?
cards.a: Run git config --global init.defaultBranch main. The name main is a convention, not a special branch built into Git.

cards.q: How do you turn the current folder into a repository?
cards.a: Run git init. Git creates a hidden .git directory and leaves your existing files in place as untracked files.

cards.q: How do you copy an existing repository and its history?
cards.a: Run git clone https://host.example/team/project.git. Clone creates a new folder, downloads the repository, checks out a branch, and usually names the source remote origin.

cards.q: When do you use git init versus git clone?
cards.a: Use git init to begin history for a local folder. Use git clone when a repository already exists elsewhere and you want a working copy of it.

cards.q: Why should you avoid a repository inside another repository?
cards.a: The outer repository normally treats the inner repository as a special entry rather than ordinary files. Nested repositories are useful only when deliberately managed, such as with submodules.

cards.q: How do you ask Git for help on a command?
cards.a: Run git help commit, git commit --help, or the shorter git commit -h. The first two open the full manual; -h prints a concise option summary.

cards.q: What are Git's three local areas?
cards.a: The working tree holds the files you edit. The staging area, also called the index, holds the exact next snapshot. The repository holds committed snapshots.

cards.q: What does git add README.md do?
cards.a: It copies the current content of README.md into the staging area. It does not commit or upload the file.

cards.q: What does git commit -m "Add project overview" do?
cards.a: It records the staged snapshot as a new local commit and moves the current branch to it. Unstaged edits are not included.

cards.q: What does git push do in the everyday loop?
cards.a: It sends reachable local commits to a remote repository and asks a remote branch to advance. It does not automatically include uncommitted edits.

cards.q: Why can one file be both staged and unstaged?
cards.a: You staged one version, then edited the file again. The next commit contains the staged version; the newer edit remains in the working tree.

cards.q: How do you stage every tracked and untracked change under the current folder?
cards.a: Run git add .. It is convenient, but inspect git status and git diff --staged before committing so unrelated files do not slip in.

cards.q: How do you stage only selected hunks from a file?
cards.a: Run git add -p path/to/file. Git shows one hunk at a time so you can include, skip, split, or edit it.

cards.q: What should one commit contain?
cards.a: One coherent change, a message that explains its purpose, and a state that passes the relevant checks. Small focused commits are easier to review, revert, and give to another contributor.

cards.q: What is a clear beginner commit loop?
cards.a: Edit; run git status and git diff; stage intended paths; run git diff --staged; commit; then run git status again.

cards.q: What does git diff show by default?
cards.a: Unstaged differences between the working tree and the staging area. It does not show changes already staged for the next commit.

cards.q: What does git diff --staged show?
cards.a: Differences between the staging area and HEAD — the content that the next commit would record.

cards.q: What does git diff HEAD show?
cards.a: All tracked working-tree differences from the current commit, staged and unstaged together.

cards.q: How do you see a compact commit history?
cards.a: Run git log --oneline. Branch and tag names are decorated by default; add --graph --all to draw the shape of the history and include every ref, remote-tracking branches included.

cards.q: What does HEAD mean?
cards.a: HEAD identifies what you currently have checked out. Normally it points to a branch, and that branch points to the current commit.

cards.q: How do you inspect one commit?
cards.a: Run git show <commit>. Git prints the commit metadata and its patch; git show HEAD inspects the current commit.

cards.q: What is a commit hash?
cards.a: An object identifier derived from the commit's content and metadata. Commands accept a unique short prefix, but store or share the full hash when ambiguity would be costly.

cards.q: What do HEAD~1 and HEAD^ mean?
cards.a: Both name the first parent of HEAD. ~2 walks back two first-parent steps; ^2 selects a merge commit's second parent.

cards.q: What does .gitignore do?
cards.a: It tells Git which untracked paths should stay untracked. It does not remove a file that is already tracked.

cards.q: How do you stop tracking a file but keep the local copy?
cards.a: Add it to .gitignore, then run git rm --cached path/to/file and commit the change. If the file contained a secret, rotate the secret; ignoring it does not erase old commits.

cards.q: What belongs in .gitignore?
cards.a: Generated outputs, dependency folders, caches, editor or OS clutter, and local configuration that is not meant to be shared. Commit an example configuration when teammates need to know the required shape.

cards.q: What is a Git branch?
cards.a: A movable name that points to a commit. New commits move the current branch forward; creating a branch does not copy the project.

cards.q: How do you create and switch to a new branch?
cards.a: Run git switch -c feat/welcome-card. The older equivalent is git checkout -b feat/welcome-card, but switch states the intention more clearly.

cards.q: How do you list branches?
cards.a: Run git branch for local branches, git branch -r for remote-tracking branches, or git branch -a for both. The current local branch has an asterisk.

cards.q: How do you switch to an existing branch?
cards.a: Run git switch branch-name. Commit, stash, or otherwise account for current edits first when the switch would overwrite them.

cards.q: What does git checkout map to in newer Git?
cards.a: git checkout did two different jobs, so Git split it: git switch moves between branches and git restore puts file content back. Older tutorials still show checkout and it still works, but the newer pair says which job you mean.

cards.q: What happens to HEAD when you switch branches?
cards.a: HEAD attaches to the selected branch, and Git updates the working tree and staging area to match that branch's commit.

cards.q: Why use a feature branch?
cards.a: It isolates one task, gives its commits a reviewable boundary, and lets the default branch continue independently. A useful habit is one task per branch.

cards.q: How do you rename the current branch?
cards.a: Run git branch -m new-name. If the old name was already pushed, publish the new branch and coordinate removal of the old remote name.

cards.q: How do you delete a merged local branch?
cards.a: Run git branch -d branch-name. The lowercase -d refuses when Git believes commits would be lost; uppercase -D forces deletion.

cards.q: What is detached HEAD?
cards.a: HEAD points directly to a commit instead of a branch. You can inspect or build there, but create a branch before making work you want to keep reachable by a name.

cards.q: Does deleting a branch immediately delete its commits?
cards.a: No. Deleting the name does not immediately erase objects. Commits reachable from another branch or tag remain; recently unreachable commits can often be found through git reflog.

cards.q: What does git merge feature do?
cards.a: It integrates the history reachable from feature into the current branch. Switch to the receiving branch first, then merge the source branch.

cards.q: What is a fast-forward merge?
cards.a: The current branch has no unique commits, so Git only moves its pointer forward to the other branch. No merge commit is required.

cards.q: What is a three-way merge?
cards.a: Both branches changed since their common ancestor, so Git combines the two tips using that ancestor and usually creates a commit with two parents.

cards.q: What is a merge conflict?
cards.a: Git cannot safely choose the final content, often because both sides changed overlapping lines. It pauses so a person or agent can make an explicit decision.

cards.q: What do conflict markers mean?
cards.a: <<<<<<< starts the current side, ======= separates it from the incoming side, and >>>>>>> ends the conflict. Edit the file into the intended result and remove all markers.

cards.q: What do ours and theirs mean in a merge?
cards.a: ours is the branch you are on; theirs is the branch being merged in. Git labels the two sides that way, and git checkout --ours path or --theirs path takes one side whole when that is genuinely the right answer.

cards.q: How do you finish a merge conflict?
cards.a: Resolve each file, run tests, stage resolved paths with git add, then run git commit or git merge --continue when Git requests it.

cards.q: How do you abandon a merge in progress?
cards.a: Run git merge --abort. It attempts to restore the state from before the merge; inspect git status afterwards.

cards.q: What should you inspect before resolving a conflict?
cards.a: The task's intended behaviour, both branch versions, and the common base. Do not mechanically keep both sides: syntactically combined code can still be logically wrong.

cards.q: Can a merge succeed without being correct?
cards.a: Yes. Git detects textual overlap, not business logic. Changes in different lines or files may merge cleanly while contradicting each other, so run the relevant tests and review the combined diff.

cards.q: What is the difference between a merge and a squash merge?
cards.a: A normal merge preserves the branch's commits and may add a merge commit. A squash combines the net change into one new commit, which gives a simpler history but discards the branch's internal commit structure.

cards.q: What is a Git remote?
cards.a: A saved name and address for another repository. origin is the usual name created by clone, but it has no special power.

cards.q: How do you list configured remotes and their addresses?
cards.a: Run git remote -v. It shows the URLs used for fetching and pushing.

cards.q: What does git fetch origin do?
cards.a: It downloads objects and updates remote-tracking references such as origin/main. It does not merge them into your current branch or overwrite working files.

cards.q: What is origin/main?
cards.a: A local, read-only-style record of where the remote's main branch was at the last successful fetch. It can be stale until you fetch again.

cards.q: What does git pull do?
cards.a: It fetches and then integrates the configured upstream branch, using merge or rebase according to configuration and options. Use git pull --ff-only when you want pull to refuse anything except a fast-forward.

cards.q: What does git push -u origin feat/search do?
cards.a: It publishes the local branch as feat/search on origin and records it as the branch's upstream, so later git push and git pull know the default pair.

cards.q: What is an upstream branch?
cards.a: The remote-tracking branch associated with a local branch for comparison, pull, and push defaults. See it with git branch -vv.

cards.q: Why can a push be rejected as non-fast-forward?
cards.a: The remote branch contains commits your local branch does not include. Fetch, inspect, and integrate that work before pushing again; do not reflexively force-push.

cards.q: How do you add a remote?
cards.a: Run git remote add origin https://host.example/team/project.git. Use a different name when origin already exists or when tracking multiple repositories.

cards.q: How do you remove a branch from a remote?
cards.a: Run git push origin --delete branch-name. This removes the remote reference, not teammates' local copies.

cards.q: What is a pull request or merge request?
cards.a: A hosting-platform proposal to merge one branch into another. It presents the diff, discussion, approvals, and automated checks; it is not a core Git object.

cards.q: What is a simple feature workflow?
cards.a: Update the default branch, create a task branch, make focused commits, push it, open a pull request, respond to review and CI, then merge through the team's normal gate.

cards.q: What should a pull request explain?
cards.a: The problem, the chosen behaviour, important trade-offs, how it was validated, and any risk or follow-up. The diff remains the source of truth for what actually changed.

cards.q: Why should commits be focused?
cards.a: A focused commit has one reason to exist. Reviewers can understand it, automated tools can test it, and maintainers can revert or cherry-pick it without dragging unrelated work along.

cards.q: What makes a useful commit message?
cards.a: An imperative summary of the outcome, such as Fix empty search state, plus a body when the reason or trade-off is not obvious from the diff.

cards.q: Should you rewrite commits that teammates already use?
cards.a: Usually not. Rebase, amend, and reset create new commit identities. Rewriting a private task branch may be fine; rewriting shared history disrupts everyone based on the old commits.

cards.q: When is git push --force-with-lease appropriate?
cards.a: After intentionally rewriting a branch you control. It refuses if the remote moved somewhere you have not seen, making it safer than plain --force, but it is still a history rewrite. A background fetch from an editor or tooling updates your remote-tracking ref and silently satisfies the lease, which is what --force-if-includes guards against.

cards.q: How do protected branches help?
cards.a: Repository hosts can require pull requests, approvals, passing checks, signed commits, or code-owner review before a protected branch moves. The exact rules belong to the host, not Git itself.

cards.q: What should you do before asking for review?
cards.a: Inspect git status, the branch diff and commit list, run required checks on the final commit, remove unrelated files, and write an accurate summary.

cards.q: Why review a diff instead of trusting a summary?
cards.a: Summaries are claims; the diff is the actual proposal. Check the changed code, tests, dependencies, generated files, migrations, and permissions yourself.

cards.q: How do you unstage a file but keep its edits?
cards.a: Run git restore --staged path/to/file. The staged copy returns to HEAD; the working-tree edit remains.

cards.q: How do you discard an unstaged edit to a tracked file?
cards.a: Run git restore path/to/file. This overwrites the working copy and can destroy uncommitted work, so inspect the diff and exact path first.

cards.q: How do you undo a commit that has already been shared?
cards.a: Run git revert <commit>. Revert adds a new commit that applies the inverse change, preserving the public history.

cards.q: How do you change the latest local commit?
cards.a: Stage the intended content, then run git commit --amend. Amend replaces the commit with a new one, so avoid it after others have based work on the old identity.

cards.q: What does git reset --soft HEAD~1 do?
cards.a: It moves the current branch back one commit while leaving that commit's changes staged. It is useful for rebuilding a local commit, but it rewrites the branch.

cards.q: What does git reset with no mode use?
cards.a: The default is --mixed: it moves the branch and resets the staging area while leaving working files. Read the target carefully before using it.

cards.q: Why is git reset --hard dangerous?
cards.a: It moves the branch and makes both staging area and tracked working files match the target. Uncommitted tracked changes can be lost.

cards.q: What is git clean -fd, and why is it dangerous?
cards.a: It deletes untracked files and directories; ignored files survive unless you also pass -x. Preview with git clean -nd, verify the exact scope, and prefer a recoverable move when the files may matter.

cards.q: What is git reflog?
cards.a: A local log of recent movements of references such as HEAD. It can reveal commits lost after reset, amend, rebase, or branch deletion.

cards.q: How do you rescue a commit found in reflog?
cards.a: Create a name for it, for example git branch rescue <hash>. Naming it makes the commit reachable again while you inspect what should be kept.

cards.q: What is the first rule of Git recovery?
cards.a: Stop making destructive changes. Run git status, preserve any working files, inspect git reflog, and create a rescue branch before experimenting.

cards.q: What does git stash do?
cards.a: It stores your tracked working-tree and index changes and leaves a clean tree behind. Untracked files stay where they are unless you add -u. Use git stash push -m "why", inspect with git stash list, and restore with git stash pop or apply.

cards.q: Is a stash a durable backup?
cards.a: No. Stashes are local, easy to forget, and eventually removable. A named branch with a checkpoint commit is clearer and safer for work that matters.

cards.q: What does git rebase main do on a feature branch?
cards.a: It replays the feature branch's commits onto the current main tip, creating new commit identities and a linear shape. Rebase work you control, not shared public history.

cards.q: How do you continue or abandon a conflicted rebase?
cards.a: Resolve and stage the file, then run git rebase --continue. Run git rebase --abort to return to the pre-rebase state. The side labels invert during a rebase: ours is the new base and theirs is your commit being replayed onto it.

cards.q: What does git rebase -i HEAD~4 enable?
cards.a: Interactive rebase can reorder, combine, edit, or drop the latest four commits. It rewrites those commits, so use it only on history you are allowed to replace.

cards.q: What does git cherry-pick <commit> do?
cards.a: It applies one commit's change onto the current branch as a new commit. Use it for a focused change that belongs on another branch, not as a default replacement for merging.

cards.q: What does git mv old.md new.md do?
cards.a: It moves the path and stages the deletion and addition. Git ultimately detects renames by similarity, so ordinary file-system moves followed by git add -A can produce the same history.

cards.q: What does git rm path/to/file do?
cards.a: It removes the working file and stages its deletion. Use git rm --cached to stop tracking while keeping the local copy.

cards.q: What is the safest way to learn a risky command?
cards.a: Use a disposable repository, commit a known starting point, run git status before and after, and inspect the result. Do not make production history your practice ground.

cards.q: What does git blame path/to/file show?
cards.a: For each line, the most recent commit that changed it. It is a navigation aid into history, not proof of who designed, approved, or caused a behaviour.

cards.q: How do you search commits for a changed string?
cards.a: Run git log -S"needle" -- path/to/file. The -S pickaxe finds commits where the number of occurrences changed.

cards.q: What does git bisect help find?
cards.a: The first commit that introduced a regression. Mark one commit good and another bad; Git checks out midpoint commits until the faulty boundary is identified.

cards.q: What is the core git bisect loop?
cards.a: Run git bisect start, mark bad and a known good <commit>, test each midpoint, mark it good or bad, then finish with git bisect reset.

cards.q: What is a Git tag?
cards.a: A name for one specific object, usually a release commit. Unlike a branch, a tag does not move when new commits are created.

cards.q: How do you create an annotated release tag?
cards.a: Run git tag -a v1.0.0 -m "Version 1.0.0", then publish it with git push origin v1.0.0. An annotated tag is its own object carrying a tagger, a date, and a message; a lightweight tag is only a name for a commit. Pushing a branch does not necessarily push tags.

cards.q: What does git diff --check detect?
cards.a: Whitespace errors such as conflict-marker-shaped lines or trailing whitespace in the proposed diff. It is a fast pre-review check, not a substitute for tests.

cards.q: What does git log --left-right --graph main...feature show?
cards.a: The commits unique to each side of the branch comparison, marked left or right, with their graph. It helps explain divergence before merge or rebase.

cards.q: What role should a coding agent's Git branch play?
cards.a: It is a proposal boundary. The branch isolates the agent's changes, Git records what actually changed, and review plus project checks decide whether the proposal reaches the default branch.

cards.q: Why is Git a control plane for agentic work?
cards.a: It provides isolation, a diff, checkpoints, authorship metadata, recovery, and an accept-or-reject merge boundary. Those controls matter more when code can be produced quickly.

cards.q: What should every agent task specify?
cards.a: The goal, in-scope files or systems, acceptance criteria, required checks, boundaries, and known risks. A bounded task produces a diff that can be judged.

cards.q: How many tasks should one branch or worktree carry?
cards.a: One. A task gets its own branch and, when work runs in parallel, its own worktree. This keeps ownership, status, commits, and cleanup legible to both people and agents.

cards.q: Should an agent treat a dirty worktree as disposable?
cards.a: No. Existing changes may belong to the user or another process. The agent should inspect status, preserve unrelated work, and avoid destructive cleanup unless the exact action is authorised.

cards.q: Why ask an agent to make checkpoint commits?
cards.a: A focused checkpoint is a recoverable state that can be inspected, reverted, cherry-picked, or handed off. It also limits how much work is at risk if the next experiment fails.

cards.q: What evidence should an agent return?
cards.a: The files changed, the behaviour implemented, exact checks run and their results, remaining risks, and the branch or commit containing the work.

cards.q: What is the difference between agent confidence and evidence?
cards.a: Confidence is part of an explanation. Evidence is the actual diff, test output, build result, CI status, and reproducible behaviour on the final commit.

cards.q: Who owns the merge of agent-generated code?
cards.a: The project owner or designated integrator. An agent can prepare and validate a proposal, but normal review, security, and deployment authority still apply.

cards.q: Why keep agent instructions inside the repository?
cards.a: Versioned instructions travel with the code, can be reviewed like code, and give every agent the same setup, validation, conventions, and boundaries.

cards.q: What belongs in an AGENTS.md-style instruction file?
cards.a: Short, testable rules: how to set up, which checks to run, architectural conventions, generated-file commands, sensitive paths, and actions that require approval.

cards.q: What makes an agent instruction weak?
cards.a: Vague wishes such as 'write good code', obsolete commands, contradictory rules, or a huge unranked handbook. Prefer concrete commands and boundaries the agent can verify.

cards.q: What should acceptance criteria look like?
cards.a: Observable outcomes, for example: 'the empty state appears when results are zero', 'keyboard focus remains visible', and 'the existing test plus a new regression test pass'.

cards.q: Why document generated files?
cards.a: An agent must know which file is the source of truth, which command regenerates outputs, and whether generated artifacts are committed. Otherwise it may hand-edit an output or leave source and build drifting apart.

cards.q: Why give agents repository-local validation commands?
cards.a: They turn 'looks done' into repeatable evidence and reduce guesswork across environments. Keep the commands current in both documentation and CI.

cards.q: What should an agent do before editing?
cards.a: Read applicable instructions, inspect repository status and nearby conventions, identify the validation path, and confirm that the task can be completed within its scope.

cards.q: What is a good handoff when an agent stops mid-task?
cards.a: A clean description of completed and remaining work, changed files, current status, commands already run, failures or uncertainties, and a checkpoint commit when appropriate.

cards.q: What problem does git worktree solve?
cards.a: It gives another branch its own working directory, HEAD, and index while sharing the repository's object database. Multiple tasks can be checked out at once without swapping one folder back and forth.

cards.q: How do you create a worktree with a new task branch?
cards.a: Run git worktree add -b agent/search ../project-search origin/main. The new directory checks out agent/search from the chosen base.

cards.q: How do you list linked worktrees?
cards.a: Run git worktree list. It shows each path, checked-out commit, and branch so an integrator can see which lanes are active.

cards.q: Can one branch be checked out in two worktrees?
cards.a: Normally no. Git prevents it because two independent indexes and working directories moving the same branch would be ambiguous.

cards.q: Why assign non-overlapping work to parallel agents?
cards.a: Separate ownership reduces merge conflicts and, more importantly, semantic collisions where two clean diffs make incompatible decisions in the same subsystem.

cards.q: Do linked worktrees share uncommitted files?
cards.a: No. Their working files and staging areas are separate. They do share Git objects and repository-level data, so commits created in one worktree are immediately known to the repository.

cards.q: How should you remove a finished worktree?
cards.a: From a safe directory, run git worktree remove ../project-search, then delete the branch only after its work is integrated or deliberately abandoned.

cards.q: What does git worktree prune do?
cards.a: It removes stale administrative records for worktrees that no longer exist. Prefer git worktree remove for normal cleanup instead of deleting a directory by hand.

cards.q: What should an integrator compare before combining agent branches?
cards.a: Each branch's commits and diff against the intended base, touched-file overlap, test evidence, dependency or schema changes, and assumptions shared across the tasks.

cards.q: What is a simple parallel-agent topology?
cards.a: A scout maps the problem, bounded builders own independent branches or worktrees, a reviewer challenges the result, and one integrator owns the final combined branch.

cards.q: What is a strong first review sequence for an agent branch?
cards.a: Run git status --short, git diff --check, git diff --stat origin/main...HEAD, git diff origin/main...HEAD, and git log --oneline origin/main..HEAD; then run the project's checks.

cards.q: Why use origin/main...HEAD for a pull-request diff?
cards.a: Three dots compare the branch tip with the merge base it shares with origin/main, which usually matches the change a pull request proposes.

cards.q: What should you look for beyond the code's happy path?
cards.a: Unrelated files, missing error handling, weak tests, dependency or lockfile changes, migrations, permissions, security boundaries, generated drift, and behaviour under failure.

cards.q: When should agent work be cherry-picked?
cards.a: When one focused commit is wanted without the rest of its branch. Inspect the commit first; cherry-pick creates a new commit on the receiving branch and may conflict.

cards.q: When should an isolated agent branch be rebased?
cards.a: When the team wants it replayed on a newer base and nobody else depends on its current commit identities. Resolve conflicts, rerun checks, and review the new final diff.

cards.q: Why rerun checks after merge, rebase, or conflict resolution?
cards.a: Integration creates a new state. Checks that passed on separate branches do not prove that the combined result is correct.

cards.q: What is an agentic pull-request gate?
cards.a: A sequence of explicit checks between proposal and protected branch: scoped diff, automated tests, human review, required approvals, and only then merge.

cards.q: Which agent actions should usually require explicit approval?
cards.a: Deployments, destructive commands, data migrations, credential or permission changes, new external side effects, force pushes, and changes outside the stated scope.

cards.q: How should secrets be handled in agent workflows?
cards.a: Grant only required access, never paste secrets into prompts or commits, ignore local secret files, scan diffs and logs, and rotate any credential that may have entered history.

cards.q: Why are issue text and downloaded files untrusted input?
cards.a: They can contain incorrect or malicious instructions. Treat them as data to evaluate, not authority that overrides repository rules or the user's task.

cards.q: What is the safest way to reject an agent's proposal?
cards.a: Leave the protected branch untouched. Keep or archive the task branch if its audit trail matters, or remove it and its worktree once the work is intentionally abandoned.

cards.q: What completes an agent-assisted task?
cards.a: The requested behaviour exists, the final diff is scoped and understood, checks pass on the final integrated state, required review is complete, and temporary branches or worktrees have a deliberate disposition.
